summary: Residues, reciprocity and the arithmetic of K_2, planned from Weibel's K-book chapter III. T.3 builds the tame symbol of a discrete valuation in the roadmap's own normalisation, which is the inverse of the K-book's, proves independence of the uniformiser, bilinearity and the Steinberg relation by the case analysis of the source, and records the ramification formula; the localisation half owns the finite support of residues, the higher Milnor residues with their product signs and the transfer with its norm-residue formula, and imports the identification with the boundary of the localisation sequence from the two roadmaps that own that sequence. T.4 builds the Bass-Tate sequence for a rational function field, including the place at infinity, the Milnor transfers and their transitivity, and Weil reciprocity on a proper regular curve with its finiteness. T.5 owns the definition of the unramified subgroup by the vanishing of every finite-place tame symbol and imports every arithmetic computation of tame kernels from the roadmaps that own them, so its coverage is partial by design. T.6 owns the Dennis-Stein symbols under their invertibility hypothesis, their relations, the comparison with Steinberg symbols and the presentation theorems under the stated hypotheses. T.7 owns the statement of the symbol formula and the classical local symbols the source constructs, and imports the norm-residue map, Tate's comparison and Hilbert reciprocity from their owners. Nothing here is formalised; implementationStatus is unchecked throughout.

declarations.provides: The unit-part decomposition of a nonzero element for a surjective discrete valuation on a field: the form in which the tame symbol is computed so that no residue is taken of a nonintegral element.
The same decomposition inside a discrete valuation ring, against a chosen irreducible.
The residue map from the units of a valuation subring to the units of the residue field, the target of the tame symbol.
The unit relating two uniformisers of a discrete valuation ring, the input to independence of the symbol from the uniformiser.
The residue at a place of a function-field element of order zero, the function-field instance of the residue map.
That a function-field element has nonzero order at only finitely many places: the whole finiteness argument for the support of residues.
That a fractional ideal of a Dedekind domain has only finitely many nonzero exponents, the same finiteness in the number-field case.
The classification of the places of a rational function field as the height-one primes together with the place at infinity, which is what makes the Bass-Tate sequence include the place at infinity.
The correspondence between the places finite on a Dedekind affine model and the height-one primes, with matching valuations and residue degrees.
The sum of the products of ramification and inertia degrees over the primes above a prime is the field degree, the bookkeeping behind the norm-residue formula.
That the relative ideal norm of a principal ideal is generated by the field norm, which relates the valuation of a norm to the residue degrees.
The field norm, the degree-one case of the transfer and the target of the reciprocity product.
Transitivity of the field norm, the degree-one shadow of transitivity of the Milnor transfer.
The evaluation of a function on a divisor as a product of norms of residues, the apparatus behind the disjoint-support form of Weil reciprocity.
The order of vanishing at a codimension-one point of an integral scheme, one of the two valuations the comparison node identifies.
The square-zero extension of a ring, the test ring for the relative statements of T.6.
The Kummer map from the units of a field to the first Galois cohomology of the roots of unity, the first ingredient of the symbol formula of T.7.
The cup product from two first cohomology groups to the second, on explicit continuous cochains, the second ingredient of the symbol formula.
The unit group in which every symbol lives.
The cyclic groups in which the arithmetic answers land.

nodes.title: The tame symbol of a discrete valuation
nodes.statement: For a discrete valuation v on a field F with residue field k define the tame symbol of a pair of nonzero elements by the sign minus one to the power v(f) times v(g), times the residue of f to the power v(g) divided by g to the power v(f). The quotient inside the residue has valuation zero, and the construction is implemented through unit parts, so the residue map is never applied to a nonintegral element. In this normalisation the symbol of a unit with a uniformiser is the residue of the unit, and the symbol of a uniformiser with a unit is its inverse.
hypotheses: v is a discrete valuation on the field F, with valuation ring R, residue field k and a uniformiser.
f and g are nonzero elements of F.
proofSteps: Decompose each argument as a unit times a power of the uniformiser, using the pinned decomposition for a surjective discrete valuation.
Form the displayed combination in terms of the two unit parts and the two valuations, so that the expression whose residue is taken is visibly a unit of the valuation ring.
Apply the pinned residue map from the units of the valuation subring to the units of the residue field.
Prove that the result does not depend on the chosen decomposition, and record the normalisation on the two mixed pairs.

Record the convention explicitly against the source: the K-book's tame symbol is the inverse of this one, since it takes the residue of g to the power v(f) over f to the power v(g). The roadmap fixes this normalisation, and every comparison below states the inversion rather than silently reversing a formula.
acceptance: The symbol of a unit with a uniformiser is the residue of the unit, and the symbol of a uniformiser with a unit is its inverse; these two pin the convention.
The symbol of two units is trivial.
The residue is never applied to a nonintegral element, which is what the unit-part implementation guarantees.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 6.3. For every discrete valuation v on F there is a Steinberg symbol K_2(F) -> k_v^x, defined by partial_v({r, s}) = (-1)^{v(r)v(s)} times the residue of s^{v(r)} / r^{v(s)}. This symbol is called the tame symbol of the valuation v. The tame symbol is onto, because if u is a unit then v(u) = 0 and partial_v(pi, u) is the residue of u.
sources.match: The symbol and its surjectivity; the source's normalisation is the inverse of the roadmap's, which this node records.

nodes.title: Independence from the uniformiser
nodes.statement: The tame symbol does not depend on the chosen uniformiser: two uniformisers differ by a unit of the valuation ring, and the resulting change in the unit parts cancels in the displayed combination.
hypotheses: v is a discrete valuation with two chosen uniformisers.
proofSteps: Import the unit relating the two uniformisers.
Substitute into the unit-part decompositions of both arguments and expand the displayed combination.
Check that the contributions of the connecting unit cancel, using bilinearity of the residue map and the two exponents.
Record that the sign is unaffected, since it depends only on the valuations.
acceptance: The symbol is independent of the uniformiser, which is what makes it an invariant of the valuation.
The cancellation uses both exponents, so a proof that ignores one of them is incomplete.
The sign depends only on the valuations, not on the uniformiser.

sources.excerpt: Writing r = u_1 pi^{v_1} and s = u_2 pi^{v_2} with u_1, u_2 units, we must show that partial_v(r, s) = (-1)^{v_1 v_2} times the residue of u_2^{v_1} / u_1^{v_2} is a Steinberg symbol.
sources.match: The unit-part computation in which the uniformiser appears only through the exponents.

nodes.title: The tame symbol is bilinear and satisfies the Steinberg relation
nodes.statement: The tame symbol is bilinear in each argument and satisfies the Steinberg relation: it is trivial whenever the two arguments sum to one. It therefore descends to a surjective homomorphism from K_2(F) to the units of the residue field.
hypotheses: v is a discrete valuation on F; the arguments are nonzero.
proofSteps: Bilinearity is immediate from the unit-part expression, since both the sign and the residue are multiplicative in each exponent.

For the Steinberg relation run the four cases of the source. If the first valuation is positive the first argument lies in the maximal ideal, so the second is a unit and the symbol is the residue of the second to the power of the first valuation, which is one. The case of a positive second valuation is symmetric, and the case of two zero valuations is trivial.

If the first valuation is negative then the inverse of the first argument has positive valuation, and the quotient of one minus the argument by the argument is congruent to minus one; since the two valuations agree the sign and the residue cancel.
Apply Matsumoto's presentation, imported from the companion part, to descend the symbol to a homomorphism out of K_2(F).
Prove surjectivity from the normalisation on a mixed pair.
acceptance: The four cases of the Steinberg computation are exhaustive and are all written out.
The descended map is onto the units of the residue field.
The Steinberg relation holds in the roadmap's normalisation as well as in the source's, since the two differ by an inversion.

sources.excerpt: To see that partial_v(r, s) = 1 when r + s = 1 we consider several cases. If v_1 > 0 then r is in the maximal ideal, so s = 1 - r is a unit and partial_v(r, s) is the residue of s^{v_1}, which is 1.
sources.match: The case analysis, as displayed.

nodes.title: Behaviour under a finite extension: the ramification formula
nodes.statement: Let E be a finite extension of F and w a valuation of E over v, with ramification index e. Then for nonzero elements of F the tame symbol at w of the pair is the e-th power of the tame symbol at v, read in the units of the larger residue field. If the extension is unramified at every prime above v, the diagonal inclusion of the residue units is compatible with the product of the symbols above.
hypotheses: E is a finite extension of F, w lies over v, and e is the ramification index.
proofSteps: Use that the valuation w restricted to F is e times v, and substitute into the unit-part expression.
Deduce the displayed power formula, checking that the sign is also raised to the e-th power correctly, which is where the parity of e enters.
For the unramified case, apply the formula at each prime above v and compose with the diagonal inclusion.
acceptance: For an unramified extension the formula is the identity on residues followed by the inclusion.
The parity of the ramification index matters for the sign, and the statement records it.
The formula is about elements of the smaller field; for elements of the larger field there is no such formula, and the transfer is the right tool.

sources.excerpt: Remark 6.3.1 (Ramification). ... Then there is an integer e, called the ramification index, such that w(r) = e v(r) for every r in F. The natural map K_2(F) -> K_2(E) is compatible with the tame symbols in the sense that for every r_1, r_2 in F^x we have partial_w(r_1, r_2) = partial_v(r_1, r_2)^e in k_w^x.
sources.match: The formula and the unramified refinement, as displayed.

nodes.title: Finite support of the residues
nodes.statement: For a field with a family of discrete valuations in which every element has nonzero valuation at only finitely many members, the tame symbol of a pair of nonzero elements is trivial at all but finitely many valuations, and the same holds for a finite sum of symbols. The proof is the observation that the symbol is trivial whenever both valuations vanish.
hypotheses: The family is the set of places of a function field, or the height-one primes of a Dedekind domain.
proofSteps: Import the finiteness of the set of places at which a given element has nonzero order, in either of its two pinned forms.
Observe that the tame symbol of a pair is trivial at every valuation where both arguments have valuation zero.
Intersect the two finite exceptional sets to bound the support of a single symbol, and take a finite union for a finite sum.
Record that this is the entire finiteness argument: no deeper input is needed.
acceptance: The support of the symbol of a pair is contained in the union of the two supports.
For a finite sum of symbols the support is the union of the supports of the summands.
For two units of the ring of integers the symbol is trivial everywhere, so the support is empty.

sources.excerpt: The units R^x form the set v^{-1}(0), and the maximal ideal of R is generated by any pi in R with v(pi) = 1.
sources.match: The valuation-zero condition under which the symbol is trivial, which is the finiteness argument.

nodes.title: Higher Milnor residues and specialisation, with their product signs
nodes.statement: For a discrete valuation on F there are two surjections out of the Milnor K-group in degree n: the higher residue to the degree n minus one group of the residue field, and the specialisation map to the degree n group of the residue field, attached to a chosen uniformiser. They are determined by their values on symbols of units times powers of the uniformiser, and the product signs are those of the anticommutative algebra in which they are constructed. In degree two the residue is the tame symbol of T.3 and the specialisation is the leading-coefficient map.
hypotheses: v is a discrete valuation on F with residue field k and a chosen uniformiser.
proofSteps: Form the graded algebra over the Milnor K-theory of the residue field generated by an indeterminate in degree one, subject to the relation that its square is the symbol of minus one with it. That relation is what makes the construction work, and it is stated rather than assumed.
Define a homomorphism from the units of F to the degree-one part sending a unit times a power of the uniformiser to the class of the reduced unit plus that power times the indeterminate.
Prove that it kills the Steinberg elements, by the three cases the source performs: both arguments units, one argument of positive valuation, and one argument outside the valuation ring.
Extend to a graded ring map by the presentation of Milnor K-theory, and split the target degreewise into the two summands to obtain the two maps.
Prove the displayed formulas on symbols and the product signs, and identify the degree-two cases with the symbols of T.3, recording the inversion between the two normalisations.
Prove surjectivity of both maps, and the dependence of the specialisation on the uniformiser.
acceptance: In degree two the residue is the tame symbol, up to the recorded inversion of conventions.
The specialisation map depends on the chosen uniformiser and the residue does not; both facts are stated.
Both maps are onto.
Without the relation on the indeterminate the map does not kill the Steinberg elements, which is the acceptance test.

nodes.title: Rigidity for a complete discretely valued field
nodes.statement: If F is complete for the valuation, with residue field k, then for every integer q prime to the characteristic of k the pair consisting of the specialisation map and the residue is an isomorphism from the Milnor K-group modulo q onto the direct sum of the corresponding groups of the residue field, in every degree.

proofSteps: State the map as the pair of the two maps of the previous node, reduced modulo q.
Prove the isomorphism in the stated range, following the source.
Record the hypothesis: without primality to the residue characteristic the statement fails, so the wild case is excluded.
acceptance: The statement is modulo q, not integrally.
The hypothesis on q is necessary.
In degree one the statement is the decomposition of the unit group of a complete discretely valued field modulo q.

nodes.title: The transfer for a finite extension, and the norm-residue formula
nodes.statement: For a finite extension of fields with a valuation on each, construct the transfer on Milnor K-theory and prove the norm-residue formula relating the residue after transfer to the norm of the residues, with the ramification indices and residue degrees appearing explicitly. Prove that restriction followed by transfer is multiplication by the degree of the extension, and the projection formula.
hypotheses: E is a finite extension of F; the valuations of E above a valuation of F are given with their ramification and inertia data.
proofSteps: Construct the transfer, in the rational-function-field case from the Bass-Tate sequence of T.4 and in general by decomposing the extension into simple ones; prove independence of the decomposition, which is the hard part and is where transitivity is needed.
State and prove the norm-residue formula at a valuation: the residue of the transfer of a class is the product over the valuations above of the norms of the residues, with the appropriate exponents.
Prove the projection formula, which expresses the transfer of a product with a restricted class.
Prove that restriction followed by transfer is multiplication by the degree, using the degree-one case, the pinned sum of the products of ramification and inertia degrees, and the projection formula.
Record that in degree one all of this is the field norm and its transitivity, both pinned.
acceptance: In degree one the transfer is the field norm and the composite is the degree, which the pinned statements give.
The norm-residue formula reduces to the ramification formula of T.3 when the class comes from the smaller field.
Transitivity holds, which is what makes the transfer independent of the chosen decomposition.

nodes.title: Identification with the boundary of the localisation sequence
nodes.statement: The tame symbol is the boundary map of the K-theory localisation sequence of a discrete valuation ring in degree two, with the sign fixed at the comparison. The localisation sequence itself is constructed by SchemeKTheoryOperations S.3 and specialised to curves by EllipticKTheory E.3; this node states the comparison, names the sign, and does not build a second localisation sequence.

proofSteps: State the localisation sequence for the discrete valuation ring, imported from its owner.
State the comparison: on a symbol of two nonzero elements the boundary is the tame symbol, with the sign recorded.
Fix the sign at the comparison rather than adjusting the symbol formula, which is the discipline the roadmap requires.

Record the two consequences: the finite support of T.3 is the statement that a class has trivial boundary at almost every point, and the exactness of the tame-kernel sequence of T.5 is a special case of the localisation sequence.
acceptance: The comparison determines the sign; a different sign convention on either side changes it, and the node says which is which.
The comparison is stated for degree two, where both sides are constructed.

nodes.title: The Bass-Tate sequence for a rational function field
nodes.statement: For a field F and the rational function field in one variable there is an exact sequence whose first map is the inclusion of the Milnor K-theory of F and whose second is the sum of the residues at the closed points of the affine line, in every degree. The place at infinity is not one of those closed points, and the sequence together with the residue at infinity is what yields the reciprocity formula for the projective line; the polynomial primes alone do not.
hypotheses: F is a field; the function field is the rational one in one variable.
proofSteps: Import the classification of the places of a rational function field as the height-one primes of the polynomial ring together with the place at infinity.
Construct the sum of the residues at the finite places, using the higher residues of T.3, and prove that it is well defined by the finite-support lemma.
Prove exactness at the two spots, following the source's filtration of Milnor K-theory of the function field by the degrees of the polynomials involved.
Prove that the sequence splits, and record the splitting the specialisation maps give.
State the role of the place at infinity: the residue there is determined by the finite residues through the reciprocity relation of the next node, and the sequence as stated omits it.
acceptance: In degree one the sequence is the divisor sequence of the affine line.
The place at infinity is omitted from the sum, which is why the sequence alone does not give reciprocity.
Exactness fails if the residues are taken over all places including infinity, which is a non-example the statement records.

nodes.title: Milnor transfers from the Bass-Tate sequence, and their transitivity
nodes.statement: Use the Bass-Tate sequence to construct the transfer along a finite extension generated by one element, and extend to an arbitrary finite extension by decomposing it into simple extensions. Prove that the result does not depend on the decomposition, which is transitivity of the transfer.
hypotheses: E is a finite extension of F, generated by finitely many elements.
proofSteps: For a simple extension, identify E with a quotient of the polynomial ring by an irreducible polynomial, so that the residue of the Bass-Tate sequence at the corresponding place provides a map out of the Milnor K-theory of the function field.
Define the transfer as the composite determined by that residue, following the source.
For a general finite extension compose the transfers of a chain of simple extensions.
Prove independence of the chain, which is the substance; record that this is what transitivity means and that it is not automatic.
Record the degree-one case, where the transfer is the field norm and transitivity is the pinned statement.
acceptance: In degree one the transfer is the field norm and transitivity is pinned.
Independence of the decomposition is a theorem and is proved, not assumed.
The construction needs the place at infinity of the Bass-Tate sequence to be handled, which is why the previous node records it.

nodes.title: Weil reciprocity on a proper regular curve
nodes.statement: For a proper regular curve over a field and two nonzero rational functions on it, the product over the closed points of the norms to the base field of the tame symbols at those points is trivial. Only finitely many factors differ from one.
hypotheses: X is a proper regular curve over F; f and g are nonzero rational functions on X.
proofSteps: Reduce to the projective line by the transfer, using the norm-residue formula of T.3 and transitivity.
For the projective line, prove the relation by combining the Bass-Tate sequence with the residue at infinity, so that the residues at the finite places and the residue at infinity cancel.
Prove the finiteness statement from the finite-support lemma of T.3.

Record the relation to the disjoint-support form: when the divisors of the two functions are disjoint the product reduces to the classical statement that the evaluation of one function on the divisor of the other is symmetric, which Tau Ceti's evaluation apparatus already expresses.
Record the two consumers: EllipticKTheory and EllipticRegulators use this to construct and descend regulator classes.
acceptance: Only finitely many factors differ from one.
For the projective line the statement is the cancellation of the finite residues against the residue at infinity.
In the disjoint-support case it reduces to the classical symmetric evaluation, which is the acceptance test against the pinned apparatus.

nodes.title: The divisor valuation against the function-field place
nodes.statement: On a proper regular curve the order of vanishing at a closed point, in the sense of the order of vanishing at a codimension-one point of an integral scheme, agrees with the order at the corresponding place of the function field. The comparison is already available on affine charts through the correspondence between places finite on a Dedekind model and height-one primes; what this node adds is the gluing of charts into the closed points of the curve.
hypotheses: X is a proper regular curve with function field F.
proofSteps: State both valuations: the scheme-theoretic order of vanishing and the place order.
Import the affine comparison, which matches places finite on a Dedekind model with height-one primes, with equal valuations, orders equal to ideal multiplicities and matching residue degrees.
Glue: cover the curve by affine charts, check that the two orders agree on overlaps, and conclude for every closed point.
Record that the place at infinity of the rational function field is covered by this, since it is a closed point of the projective line.
acceptance: For the projective line the comparison covers the place at infinity.
The two orders agree at every closed point, which is what makes the reciprocity product well posed.
On an affine chart the statement is the pinned correspondence and nothing more.

nodes.title: The unramified subgroup of K_2 of a field
nodes.statement: For a field with a chosen family of discrete valuations define the unramified subgroup of K_2 to be the intersection of the kernels of the tame symbols at every member of the family. For a number field the family is the set of finite places, and the subgroup is the tame kernel. The definition makes sense before any localisation theorem and does not presuppose one.
hypotheses: F is a field with a family of discrete valuations; for the arithmetic case it is a number field and the family is its finite places.
proofSteps: Take the intersection of the kernels of the tame symbols of T.3 over the family.
Prove that the intersection is a subgroup, and that it is functorial for a field extension that carries the family into the family, using the ramification formula.
Record the finite-support lemma: for a given class only finitely many symbols are nontrivial, so membership is a finite check once a set containing the support is known.
Record what is not asserted: the identification with K_2 of the ring of integers is the localisation theorem, which ArithmeticKTheory N.2 owns and which is imported, not proved here.
acceptance: A class of K_2 of the ring of integers is unramified, which is one inclusion of the localisation theorem.
The symbol of two units of the ring of integers is unramified everywhere.
Membership is a finite check once the support is bounded, by the finite-support lemma.
The definition does not presuppose the localisation theorem, which is the discipline this layer needs.

nodes.title: The tame-kernel exact sequence, and where it is proved
nodes.statement: For a number field the sequence from the trivial group to K_2 of the ring of integers, to K_2 of the field, to the direct sum over the finite places of the units of the residue fields, and to the trivial group, is exact. The surjectivity on the right and the injectivity on the left are both part of the statement. The sequence is a special case of the K-theory localisation sequence, which ArithmeticKTheory N.2 derives; this layer states it, supplies the residues it is built from, and does not prove it a second time.
hypotheses: F is a number field with ring of integers and finite places.
proofSteps: State the sequence with the tame symbols of T.3 as its third map, and record that the third map is the sum of the residues.

Record the two nontrivial halves: surjectivity, which follows from the surjectivity of each tame symbol and the finite-support lemma, and injectivity, which is the content of the localisation theorem.
Import the localisation derivation from ArithmeticKTheory N.2 and record that the S-integer variant, which allows residues at a finite set of places, belongs to SpecialValuesBirchTate B.7.
State the compatibility that makes the import legitimate: the boundary of the imported sequence is the tame symbol of T.3, with the sign fixed by the comparison node of T.3.
acceptance: The third map is surjective, which follows from the surjectivity of each symbol.
Injectivity is imported, not proved here.
The S-integer variant is imported as well, with its own statement about the orders.

This layer supplies the residues and the unramified subgroup those computations are stated with.
hypotheses: F is a number field or the rationals, as each computation requires.
proofSteps: List each computation with the layer that owns it and the form in which this layer supplies its input.

State the discipline the roadmap requires and that this node enforces: an upper bound together with a surjective presentation is not an isomorphism, and may not be reported as one without a matching lower bound or a complete kernel argument.
Record the one computation this layer does prove, namely that the symbol of two units is unramified everywhere, which is the easy inclusion of the tame-kernel sequence.
Record that K_2 of the rationals is infinite precisely because the residue sum is, which is the observation the roadmap asks to be kept visible.
acceptance: K_2 of the integers has order two and K_2 of the rationals is infinite; the two are consistent because the residue sum is infinite.
A presentation with a matching lower bound is required before an order is claimed.
None of the four computations is proved here; each is attributed.

nodes.title: Dennis-Stein symbols
nodes.statement: For commuting elements of a ring whose product differs from one by a unit, define the Dennis-Stein symbol as the displayed word in the Steinberg group; it lies in K_2 because its image in the elementary group is trivial. It is independent of the two indices, and when the first entry is a unit it equals the Steinberg symbol of that entry with one minus the product. The symbols satisfy three relations, and the modern sign convention is used, which differs from the pre-1980 literature.
hypotheses: R is an associative unital ring; the two elements commute and one minus their product is a unit.
proofSteps: Write the displayed word and check that its image in the elementary group is trivial, so that it lies in K_2.
Prove independence of the two indices.
Prove that for a unit first entry it reduces to a Steinberg symbol.
Prove the three relations: the symmetry relation, the addition relation, and the product relation.
Record the sign convention and the consequence that the symbol with a one entry is trivial.
Record the relative form: when one entry lies in an ideal the symbol is an element of the relative group, which is where these symbols are indispensable.
acceptance: The symbol with a one entry is trivial, by the product relation.
For a unit first entry it reduces to a Steinberg symbol.
The three relations hold.
The modern convention is used; the pre-1980 symbol is a different element, and mixing them is an error.

sources.match: The definition, the three relations and the warning about the convention, as displayed.

nodes.title: Presentation of K_2 under the stated hypotheses
nodes.statement: For a commutative local ring, or a field, K_2 is presented as the abelian group generated by the Dennis-Stein symbols of pairs whose product differs from one by a unit, subject only to the three relations. The presentation is asserted only under those hypotheses, and Matsumoto's theorem for fields is not extended to an arbitrary ring.
hypotheses: R is a commutative local ring or a field.
proofSteps: State the presentation and import it from the source, which attributes it to Maazen, Stienstra and van der Kallen in the form corrected by Keune.
Record the historical caveat the source gives: the earlier work preceded the correct definition of relative K_2.
Record the boundary: for a general ring neither this presentation nor Matsumoto's is asserted, and the stable-range hypotheses under which partial results are available are named rather than assumed.
Prove the compatibility with the Steinberg presentation for a field, by translating the symbols.
acceptance: For a field the two presentations agree after translation.
For a general ring nothing is asserted, which is the discipline the roadmap requires.
The three relations suffice, with no others.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 5.11.1. (a) Let R be a commutative local ring, or a field. Then K_2(R) may be presented as the abelian group generated by the symbols with r, s in R such that 1 - rs is a unit, subject only to the relations (D1), (D2) and (D3).
sources.match: The theorem and its hypotheses, as displayed.

nodes.title: Square-zero and nilpotent tests of the relative theory
nodes.statement: Test the relative statements on a square-zero extension: for an ideal with zero square the relative Dennis-Stein symbols with one entry in the ideal generate the relative K_2, and the relations simplify because the product term vanishes. Use the pinned square-zero extension as the test ring and compare the boundary maps with the low-degree symbol calculations, without extending the field presentation to an arbitrary ring.
hypotheses: R is a ring and the ideal has zero square; the test ring is the pinned square-zero extension.
proofSteps: Instantiate the relative symbols at an ideal with zero square and simplify the three relations, in which the product term drops out.
State what the simplification gives: the relative group is generated by symbols with one entry in the ideal, and the addition relation becomes additive in that entry.
Compare the boundary of the relative sequence with the symbol calculations, which is the test the consuming layer performs.
Record the prohibition: none of this extends Matsumoto's field presentation to an arbitrary ring, and the test is a test, not a general theorem.
acceptance: For a zero ideal the relative group is trivial.
For an ideal with zero square the addition relation is additive, which is the simplification the test uses.
No general-ring presentation is claimed.

nodes.title: The norm-residue symbol formula
nodes.statement: State the symbol formula for the norm-residue map: modulo m, the class of the Steinberg symbol of a and b maps to the cup product of the two Kummer classes, in the second Galois cohomology of the twice-twisted roots of unity. The map itself is constructed by MotivicEtaleKTheory M.3, which also proves Tate's local, global and S-integer comparison; this layer states the formula, supplies the two ingredients that the pinned libraries already have, and does not build a second map.
hypotheses: F is a field with m invertible in it; a and b are nonzero.
proofSteps: State the two pinned ingredients: the Kummer map from the units to the first cohomology of the roots of unity, with kernel the m-th powers, and the cup product from two first cohomology groups to the second for an equivariant continuous biadditive pairing.

Record the one thing the pinned libraries lack: the coefficient module of the twice-twisted roots of unity, or any named root-of-unity pairing, without which the cup product has no target; this is what the request asks for.
State the formula and the compatibility with the Steinberg relation, which on the cohomological side is the statement that the cup product of the Kummer classes of a and one minus a vanishes.
Record the agreement with the etale Chern class as a statement of the owning layer, not of this one.
acceptance: The formula is the statement that the symbol goes to the cup product; the map is imported.
The Steinberg relation on the cohomological side is the vanishing of the cup product of the Kummer classes of a and one minus a.
The pinned libraries supply both ingredients but not the twisted coefficient module, which the request names.

sources.excerpt: The Steinberg identity (a, 1 - a)_F = 1 is proven by noting that (1 - a) is a norm from the intermediate field E = F(x), x^m = a.
sources.match: The Steinberg identity for the norm-residue symbol, which is the arithmetic content of the formula.

nodes.title: The classical local symbols: Hilbert and norm-residue
nodes.statement: For a local field containing one half, the Hilbert quadratic-residue symbol of a pair is plus or minus one according to whether the conic with those coefficients has a rational point. For a local field with m-th roots of unity, the m-th power norm-residue symbol is the pairing adjoint to the composite of the projection to the norm quotient with the norm-residue isomorphism of local class field theory. Both are Steinberg symbols: the Hilbert symbol trivially, because the equation has a solution when the arguments sum to one, and the norm-residue symbol by the argument the source gives. Over the reals the Hilbert symbol is the sign symbol.
hypotheses: F is a local field; for the Hilbert symbol one half lies in F, and for the norm-residue symbol the m-th roots of unity do.
proofSteps: Define the Hilbert symbol by the solvability of the displayed equation, and record that bilinearity is classical for a local field and may fail for a general field of characteristic different from two.
Prove the Steinberg identity for it, which is trivial because the two arguments summing to one give an obvious solution.
Define the norm-residue symbol through the Kummer extension and the norm-residue isomorphism of local class field theory, imported from ClassFieldTheory.
Prove the Steinberg identity for it by the norm argument the source gives: one minus a is a norm from the intermediate field obtained by adjoining an m-th root of a.
Record that the norm-residue symbol is a split surjection onto the roots of unity, with the explicit splitting the source constructs.
Record Moore's theorem as the structural statement that explains the role of the symbol, attributing the two halves of its proof as the source does.
acceptance: Over the reals the Hilbert symbol is the sign symbol.
For the 2-adic rationals the Hilbert symbol of minus one with itself is minus one, which is the source's worked example.
The norm-residue symbol is onto the roots of unity and splits.
The Hilbert symbol is a Steinberg symbol for a local field; for a general field of characteristic different from two it need not be bilinear, which is a non-example the definition records.

sources.excerpt: The Hilbert (quadratic residue) symbol on F is defined by setting c_F(r, s) equal to +1 or -1, depending on whether or not the equation rx^2 + sy^2 = 1 has a solution in F. ... Moore's Theorem 6.2.4. If F is a local field, then K_2(F) is the direct sum of a uniquely divisible abelian group and a finite cyclic group, isomorphic under the norm residue symbol to the roots of unity in F.
sources.match: The two symbols and Moore's theorem, as displayed.

nodes.title: Tate's comparison, the change-of-root rule and global reciprocity, and their owners
nodes.statement: Record the three remaining targets of the layer with the roadmaps that own them: Tate's comparison for local and global fields and its S-integer extension, owned by MotivicEtaleKTheory M.3; the identification of the local symbol with the Kummer cup product followed by the local invariant, owned by ClassFieldTheory Layer 5; and the Hilbert product formula, owned by ClassFieldTheory Layer 14. State the change-of-root rule, which is this layer's own: a primitive root is fixed only to identify a twist with a scalar coefficient module, and changing the root changes the identification by the corresponding scalar.
hypotheses: F is a local or global field; m is invertible in F and the m-th roots of unity lie in F for the identification.
proofSteps: State the change-of-root rule precisely: the identification of the twice-twisted coefficient module with the scalar one depends on the chosen primitive root, and two choices differ by the ratio, which acts on the identification in the displayed way.
State each of the three imported results with its owner and the form in which this layer's symbols enter it.

Record the prohibition the roadmap states: the comparison over a ring must go through the actual etale localisation sequence, and not through a blanket assertion that etale cohomology of a scheme is Galois cohomology of its function field.
Record the one thing this layer supplies to all three: the tame symbols and the unramified subgroup in which the ring-level statements are phrased.
acceptance: The change-of-root rule is stated and is this layer's own.
The three comparisons are attributed, not reproved.
The ring-level statement is not obtained by the blanket assertion the roadmap forbids.

sources.excerpt: Since a primitive m-th root of unity zeta is not a norm from K, it follows that there is an x in F such that (zeta, x)_F is not 1. Therefore the norm residue symbol is a split surjection with inverse zeta^i -> {zeta^i, x}.
sources.match: The role of a chosen primitive root, which is what the change-of-root rule is about.

coverage.note: The umbrella stage: its two sub-stages carry the work and no node realises it directly.

The tame symbol in the roadmap's normalisation, implemented through unit parts so that no residue is taken of a nonintegral element; independence from the uniformiser; bilinearity and the Steinberg relation by the four-case analysis of the source; the normalisation on the two mixed pairs; and the ramification formula for a finite extension. The inversion between this normalisation and the source's is recorded in the definition and in a unit test, rather than reconciled silently.

Finite support of the residues, the higher Milnor residues and specialisation maps with their product signs, rigidity for a complete field, the transfer with the norm-residue formula and the projection formula, and the identification with the boundary of the localisation sequence, whose construction is imported from the two roadmaps that own it with the sign fixed at the comparison.

The Bass-Tate sequence with the place at infinity kept outside the sum and its role recorded, the Milnor transfers with transitivity, Weil reciprocity on a proper regular curve with its finiteness and its reduction to the projective line, and the comparison of the divisor valuation with the function-field place, which is pinned on affine charts and glued here.

This layer owns the definition of the unramified subgroup by the simultaneous vanishing of the finite-place tame symbols, and supplies the residues every arithmetic statement is phrased with. Every computation the layer's targets name is owned elsewhere and is imported: the localisation theorem by ArithmeticKTheory N.2, the certified presentations by N.6, K_2 of the integers and of the rationals by N.8, the S-integer comparison by SpecialValuesBirchTate B.7, and K_2 of a finite field by KTheoryFiniteLocalFields L.1 and by the companion part of this roadmap. The coverage is partial by design, not by omission.
remaining: The injectivity half of the tame-kernel sequence, which is the localisation theorem and belongs to ArithmeticKTheory N.2.
Certified finite presentations with matching lower bounds, which belong to ArithmeticKTheory N.6.

coverage.note: The Dennis-Stein symbols under their invertibility hypothesis with the modern sign convention recorded, their three relations, the comparison with Steinberg symbols when the entries are units, the presentation theorem under the local-ring and field hypotheses only, and the square-zero test of the relative theory. Matsumoto's field presentation is explicitly not extended to an arbitrary ring.

This layer owns the statement of the symbol formula, the two classical local symbols with their Steinberg identities and Moore's structure theorem, and the change-of-root rule. The norm-residue map itself, Tate's comparison for local and global fields and its S-integer extension, the identification with the local invariant, and the Hilbert product formula are owned by MotivicEtaleKTheory M.3 and by two layers of ClassFieldTheory, and are imported. The coverage is partial by design.
remaining: The norm-residue map and Tate's comparison, owned by MotivicEtaleKTheory M.3.
The comparison with the local invariant and the Hilbert product formula, owned by ClassFieldTheory Layers 5 and 14.
The coefficient module of the twice-twisted roots of unity, which neither pinned library has and which the request names.

gaps.title: Bass and Tate are cited, not obtained
gaps.detail: The exact sequence for a rational function field, the construction of the Milnor transfers from it and their transitivity are attributed by the source to Bass and Tate, whose paper was not obtained. The nodes state them with the attribution and set out the proof architecture the source describes; a continuation that obtains the paper should decompose the transitivity argument, which is the substantial part.

gaps.title: Weil reciprocity is proved from the Bass-Tate sequence, not from a source that states it
gaps.detail: The K-book does not state Weil reciprocity in the symbol form the roadmap asks for. The node reduces it to the projective line by the transfer and derives it there from the Bass-Tate sequence together with the residue at infinity, which is the standard argument; no source was obtained that states the curve form, so the derivation is written out rather than cited.

gaps.title: The gluing of the two valuations is not in the pinned libraries
gaps.detail: The comparison of the order of vanishing at a codimension-one point of a scheme with the order at the corresponding place of the function field is pinned on affine charts, through the correspondence between places finite on a Dedekind model and height-one primes. The gluing of charts into the closed points of a proper regular curve is not, and the node states it as work rather than citing it.

gaps.title: The twisted coefficient module is missing from both libraries
gaps.detail: The pinned libraries have the Kummer map and the cup product from two first cohomology groups to the second, but no coefficient module of the twice-twisted roots of unity and no named root-of-unity pairing, so the cup product of two Kummer classes has no target. T.7's symbol formula is stated against that missing module and the request names it.

restructure.title: Two groups of nodes moved out of the companion T.1 part
restructure.detail: An earlier revision of the packet for the T.1 part of this roadmap placed the higher tame symbols with their rigidity corollary, and the Dennis-Stein symbols with their presentation theorem, under T.2:symbols. The roadmap assigns higher Milnor residues, specialisation with a uniformiser and their product signs to T.3:localization-comparison, and the Dennis-Stein symbols to T.6. Both groups are owned here instead, and the companion packet was corrected before review rather than left as a duplication. No restructuring of the atlas is proposed: the stage texts already say where these belong, and this entry records the correction so that a reviewer of either part can see it.
